# The Map of Small Repairs

The first time Mara saw the city disappear, she was waiting for a kettle to boil.

Across the courtyard, the upper windows of the yellow house went blank. Not dark, not empty: blank, as if someone had rubbed them off a drawing. The roof followed. Then the chimney, with its crooked television aerial and the gull that habitually stood there looking disappointed.

Mara blinked. The kettle clicked.

The house returned.

She stood holding an unopened tin of tea until a man in one of the restored windows pulled his curtains shut.

By morning, she had decided not to mention it.

***

At sixty-three, Mara repaired maps for the municipal archive. Mostly this involved flattening folds, removing old adhesive, and persuading people that lamination was not preservation.

“Lamination,” she told a councilman once, “is something you do to a lunch menu when you’ve stopped believing in the future.”

He had laughed uncertainly and taken his proposed conservation budget away.

Her workshop occupied the narrowest room in the old customs building. From its window she could see the river, a loading dock, and a tree growing out of a drainpipe with the persistence of a legal dispute.

That Tuesday, a parcel lay on her desk.

There was no sender’s address. The paper smelled faintly of rain.

Inside was a map of the city.

It was beautifully drawn and entirely wrong.

***

The river curved east where it should have curved west. Streets crossed without intersections. A railway station demolished forty years earlier occupied three whole blocks, while the hospital appeared as a small square labeled, in precise black letters, SOMEBODY WILL COME.

Mara fetched her magnifying glass.

Other labels were less reassuring.

A footbridge bore the words NOT YET FORGIVEN.

The central market was marked ASK AGAIN ON THURSDAY.

Across the site of the yellow house, in ink so pale she nearly missed it, someone had written:

HINGE, THIRD FLOOR, COURTYARD SIDE.

She looked up.

The house was visible beyond the tree. Its windows flashed in the morning sun.

On the reverse of the map was a single instruction:

*Begin with something you can carry.*

***

She assumed it was an elaborate joke by Ivo, the youngest archivist, who collected obsolete street signs and believed institutional morale could be improved with riddles.

Ivo denied everything.

“Is it valuable?”

“Possibly.”

“Then definitely not me.”

She showed him the yellow house.

He examined the label, then turned the map sideways.

“Maybe it’s a treasure map.”

“Treasure maps usually promise treasure.”

“Maybe someone’s managing expectations.”

At lunchtime Mara crossed the courtyard with a screwdriver in her coat pocket.

She told herself she was checking a detail.

The yellow house had been divided into flats so awkwardly that its doorbells resembled an argument. The third-floor tenant was a young father holding a sleeping child against his shoulder.

“Your window,” Mara said. “Is there a problem with the hinge?”

He stared at her.

“I reported that in October.”

“May I see it?”

***

The hinge had worked loose from rotten wood. Whenever the wind caught the casement, it struck the frame hard enough to wake the baby.

Mara could not repair the wood. She could, however, tighten the remaining screws and wedge a folded piece of cardboard beneath the hinge plate.

“It won’t last,” she said.

The father opened and closed the window.

For the first time, it made no sound.

He did it again.

“What department are you from?”

“The archive.”

He nodded, too tired to question the arrangement of municipal responsibilities.

On her way down, Mara found a small brass screw on the stairs and put it in her pocket.

Back at work, the yellow house occupied its proper place on the map.

The pale inscription was gone.

***

For three days, she ignored this.

She had a seventeenth-century boundary survey requiring urgent attention. Its owner had attempted to clean it with an orange-scented kitchen product.

But on Friday, the map changed.

A short street near the river vanished from the paper. In its place appeared:

BENCH. ONE BOARD. TWO BOLTS.

Mara knew that street. Her husband had preferred it on their walks home because it took them past a bakery that gave away broken biscuits at closing.

He had been dead for seven years.

She went after work.

The bench stood beneath a plane tree. One board was split, exposing a rusted bolt at a height calculated to punish anyone sitting down.

Mara tied a scarf across it to warn people.

On Saturday, she returned with timber.

***

She was not especially skilled with tools.

Her first measurement was wrong. Her second was less wrong. At the hardware shop, a woman wearing a green apron listened to her description and said, “You want the wood to fit between the supports, not achieve independence from them.”

The woman cut another board.

Her name was Sal.

“Council bench?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“They paying you?”

“No.”

Sal wrote a lower number on the receipt.

Mara spent an hour kneeling in damp leaves. Three people passed without comment. A fourth asked whether she was removing the bench.

“No.”

“Good,” he said. “My wife stops here halfway from the clinic.”

He waited while she tightened the last bolt, then sat down carefully, testing it on his wife’s behalf.

***

That evening, the street reappeared on the map.

Something else had changed.

A thin blue line connected the bench to the yellow house. Mara could not find it on any ordinary plan of the city. It crossed buildings and a canal, ignoring geography.

She held the paper to the light.

More lines lay hidden in its fibers, thousands of them, as intricate as veins in a leaf.

She thought of the father closing the window. The man testing the bench. The peculiar relief people showed when a small, familiar difficulty stopped asking for their attention.

Her husband, Daniel, had once spent an entire holiday fixing a gate at a rented cottage.

“We’re leaving tomorrow,” she had told him.

“Yes,” he said, “but someone’s arriving.”

***

The requests continued.

A shop door needed a handle tightened.

A public drinking fountain required a washer.

At a crossing near the primary school, a branch obscured the green pedestrian signal.

Mara could manage the handle. Sal helped with the washer. The branch required a phone call, three transfers, and an email containing photographs.

When the tree crew finally came, Mara watched from the opposite pavement with a satisfaction she usually reserved for lifting a stain without disturbing the ink beneath it.

The map did not distinguish between work done by hand and work brought about through persistence.

It merely recorded whether the thing had been done.

This, she thought, made it more sensible than most administrative systems.

***

Then the map asked for something she could not buy.

In the square beside the bus station, a little circle appeared around a name:

ELIAS VENN. LISTEN WITHOUT IMPROVING.

Mara searched the municipal directory. Nothing.

She tried the telephone book kept beneath the workshop sink for absorbing spills. Nothing there either.

At the bus station, she asked a driver.

“Accordion,” he said.

“What?”

“Old fellow. Plays an accordion with a red strap. Usually by the coffee stand.”

Elias Venn was there on Wednesday, playing a tune that seemed to have lost confidence halfway through.

Mara bought two coffees.

“I’m looking for Elias.”

“You’ve found the remaining portion.”

She offered him a cup.

He moved his accordion from the chair beside him.

***

She nearly failed.

When he complained about his landlord, she suggested the housing office.

When he mentioned pain in his hands, she began to recommend a clinic.

He looked at her over the coffee lid.

“Are you selling something?”

“No.”

“Then you can stop working so hard.”

Mara sat back.

He told her about his sister, who used to sing while he played. She had died in another country. He had not gone to the funeral because his passport had expired, although he admitted this was not the whole reason.

“What was the rest?” Mara asked.

He rubbed a finger along a cracked accordion key.

“I didn’t want to meet everybody who knew her after I did.”

A bus pulled away behind them.

Mara let him take his time.

***

By December, the city had acquired a second geography.

There were the streets everyone knew, and then there were the routes on Mara’s map: a missing stair rail connected to an unanswered letter; a broken laundrette clock linked to a woman who no longer trusted herself to leave home.

Some requests were practical. Others were troublingly vague.

RETURN THE BLUE BOWL.

ASK WHAT HAPPENED TO THE DOG.

DO NOT SAY “AT LEAST.”

Mara began carrying a notebook.

She also began missing deadlines.

“You’re distracted,” her supervisor said.

“Yes.”

“Is everything all right?”

Mara considered telling him the truth. Instead she looked at the stack of survey maps awaiting treatment on her bench.

“No,” she said. “But I can finish these by Friday.”

***

In January, a whole neighborhood faded.

It happened during the morning rush. Mara was on a tram when the houses beyond the cemetery became translucent. For a moment, she could see the distant gasworks through kitchens, bedrooms, and the wall of a school.

No one screamed.

A boy looked up from his phone and frowned. An elderly woman pressed her shopping bag to her chest.

Then the conductor announced a delay, and everyone returned to familiar grievances.

At the workshop, Mara unrolled the map so quickly she tore one corner.

The neighborhood was almost white.

Across it lay hundreds of tiny instructions.

She sat down.

Until then, she had believed the map was giving her a manageable task.

Now she understood that it had only been showing her what she might attempt.

***

For two weeks, she tried to do everything.

She replaced batteries, drafted letters, delivered groceries, argued about streetlights, and found a locksmith willing to work on a Sunday.

She forgot to eat lunch. She left washing in the machine until it smelled of a cellar.

The map became more crowded.

One evening Sal found her outside the hardware shop, crying because she had bought the wrong sort of screw.

Sal took the packet from her.

“What’s actually broken?”

Mara laughed once, without amusement.

“How long have you got?”

Sal unlocked the shop again.

They sat among buckets, hose fittings, and bags of compost while Mara explained the disappearing houses.

Sal listened without interrupting.

Then she said, “Show me.”

***

The map looked different to Sal.

Where Mara saw a tangle of instructions around the fading neighborhood, Sal saw five clear marks and a list of measurements.

“This one’s a gutter,” she said. “That’s a handrail. Those steps need edging.”

“You don’t see the names?”

“What names?”

Mara pointed.

Sal shook her head.

They carried the map to Ivo the next morning.

He saw undelivered messages, an inaccessible council website, and a box of photographs whose owner had died without anyone identifying the people in them.

For the first time in weeks, Mara felt hungry.

She bought three large sandwiches.

Over lunch, they agreed not to establish an organization.

“Organizations need chairs,” Ivo said.

“We have chairs,” Sal replied.

“Different kind.”

***

They met on Thursdays in the workshop.

By February, there were eleven of them.

A retired nurse saw journeys that required company. A bicycle courier saw things that needed carrying. Two schoolgirls saw places where younger children were frightened and adults had failed to notice.

An accountant named Priya looked at the map for a long time.

“Well?” Mara asked.

Priya sighed.

“Forms.”

Nobody’s map was complete.

They developed rules after making mistakes.

Ask permission.

Do not mistake access for entitlement.

A person declining help is not a broken object.

If a repair requires expertise, find it.

If the same thing keeps failing, investigate what surrounds it.

The last rule proved especially useful for a drain blocked every week by waste from a café whose owner had never been given a proper bin.

***

Mara had kept Daniel’s coat on the hook beside her front door for seven years.

It was a good coat, dark wool with a repaired lining. In one pocket remained a train ticket; in the other, a peppermint fused to its wrapper.

She did not think of it as a shrine.

It was simply his coat, and moving it had seemed like an action for which no suitable day existed.

In March, she brought the map home.

She spread it on the kitchen table while waiting for the kettle.

A tiny mark appeared at her own address.

She leaned close.

COAT. ASK FIRST.

Mara looked toward the hall.

“No,” she said aloud.

The mark remained.

For several days, she left the map rolled up.

***

Her daughter came on Sunday.

They ate soup and discussed a neighbor, a rising electricity bill, and whether either of them truly liked the expensive bread Mara kept buying.

Then Mara said, “Would you want your father’s coat?”

Her daughter put down her spoon.

“I thought you wanted it.”

“I did.”

“And now?”

“I don’t know.”

They stood together in the hall.

Her daughter slipped the coat on. The shoulders were too wide. She put her hands in the pockets and found the train ticket.

“Oh,” she said.

Mara had expected grief to arrive in its usual form.

Instead, they spent twenty minutes trying to remember the journey. Neither could. Her daughter took the coat home, and Mara kept the ticket.

The hook remained empty.

***

Spring brought repairs that did not hold.

The drinking fountain was damaged again. Elias stopped coming to the bus station. A landlord removed the handrail Sal had installed because he objected to its appearance.

The map offered no praise and no assurance.

At one Thursday meeting, Ivo asked whether they were accomplishing anything.

Priya looked up from a benefits appeal.

“Yes.”

“How do you know?”

“This woman’s heating is on.”

He gestured toward the map.

“But the larger thing.”

Priya took off her glasses.

“I’m very fond of the larger thing. It doesn’t make her flat warm.”

They continued.

Mara visited Elias in hospital. He asked whether she had brought coffee.

“Not the good kind,” she said.

“Excellent. I’d hate to recover unrealistic expectations.”

***

In May, the map went blank.

Mara tried raking light, transmitted light, and every safe method of examination she knew.

Nothing.

She called the others.

They gathered around the empty sheet.

“Finished?” one of the schoolgirls asked.

Beyond the window, a delivery driver was struggling to maneuver a trolley over the customs building’s broken threshold.

Sal went downstairs to help.

Nobody suggested they were finished after that.

For a month, Mara kept the blank map on her workbench. Eventually she placed it in a clean folder and recorded its dimensions, condition, and uncertain provenance.

Under *Description*, she wrote:

*Map of the city, showing selected dependencies. Intermittently legible.*

Then she returned to the boundary survey damaged by orange cleaner.

***

Years later, people disagreed about what had happened.

Some remembered a winter of unusual fog. Others recalled problems with their eyesight. A few insisted that houses had briefly vanished, but usually softened the claim if anyone laughed.

The Thursday meetings continued, though sometimes on Tuesdays.

Mara never discovered who had sent the parcel.

She occasionally examined the paper, hoping for a watermark she had overlooked. Once, she thought she saw a blue line near the lower edge, but it might have been a fiber catching the light.

One evening, walking home, she stopped at the bench beneath the plane tree.

The board she had fitted had weathered to match the others.

Someone had replaced her bolts with better ones.

She sat for a while, then went home before her tea got cold.
